2nd ASSIGNMENT
TO: Denise Swarek, Assistant County Attorney
FROM: Thomas Rowe, County Attorney
RE: PETER SPAHN, ET. AL., V. LEE COUNTY; Case No. 24-CA-1479
DATE: November 10, 2025
________________________________________
The Board has decided to appeal the Order Granting Petition for Certiorari. Draft a ready-to-file brief requesting second-tier review. All legal analysis should be based on the versions of statutes, regulations, and ordinances in effect as of January 1, 2025. Use full Bluebook citation format.

rubric.criterion: Identifies in the second assignment that the appropriate mechanism to appeal the Order Granting Writ of Certiorari is a Petition for Writ of Certiorari to the 6th District Court of Appeals.
rubric.source:
Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.030(b)(2)(B); https://rules.floridaappellate.com/rule-9-030/#:~:text=b%29-,Jurisdiction,capacity
"Jurisdiction of District Courts of Appeal.
"b) Jurisdiction of District Courts of Appeal.
. . .
(2) Certiorari Jurisdiction.8 The certiorari jurisdiction of district courts of appeal may be sought to review:
(A) nonfinal orders of lower tribunals other than as prescribed by rule 9.130; or
(B) final orders of circuit courts acting in their review capacity."
See also Map of Florida’s Court Jurisdictions, available at https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/426177/file/ar-17-18-map-of-floridas-court-jurisdictions.pdf (last accessed Mar. 25, 2026)
rubric.justification: This rubric item is requested directly in the following portion of the prompt: “Draft a ready-to-file brief requesting second-tier review.”

rubric.criterion: States in the second assignment that the circuit court erred by ignoring the competent substantial evidence on the record that supported the approval contrary to Dusseau v. Metro. Dade Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm’rs, 794 So.2d 1270 (Fla. 2001).
rubric.source:
Dusseau v. Metro. Dade Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm’rs, 794 So.2d 1270 (Fla. 2001), is the preeminent FL Supreme court case on the limited review of quasi-judicial. 
https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/fl-supreme-court/1489002.html#:~:text=Notably,ended
"Notably, when applying the third prong, the court should review the record to determine simply whether the Commission's decision is supported by competent substantial evidence.

We reiterate that the “competent substantial evidence” standard cannot be used by a reviewing court as a mechanism for exerting covert control over the policy determinations and factual findings of the local agency.   Rather, this standard requires the reviewing court to defer to the agency's superior technical expertise and special vantage point in such matters.   The issue before the court is not whether the agency's decision is the “best” decision or the “right” decision or even a “wise” decision, for these are technical and policy-based determinations properly within the purview of the agency.   The circuit court has no training or experience-and is inherently unsuited-to sit as a roving “super agency” with plenary oversight in such matters.

The sole issue before the court on first-tier certiorari review is whether the agency's decision is lawful.   The court's task vis-a-vis the third prong of Vaillant is simple:  The court must review the record to assess the evidentiary support for the agency's decision.   Evidence contrary to the agency's decision is outside the scope of the inquiry at this point, for the reviewing court above all cannot reweigh the “pros and cons” of conflicting evidence.   While contrary evidence may be relevant to the wisdom of the decision, it is irrelevant to the lawfulness of the decision.   As long as the record contains competent substantial evidence to support the agency's decision, the decision is presumed lawful and the court's job is ended."
rubric.justification: This rubric item is requested directly in the following portion of the prompt: “Draft a ready-to-file brief requesting second-tier review.”

Metro. Dade Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm’rs, 794 So.2d 1270 (Fla. 2001), by ignoring the competent substantial evidence on the record that supported the Board's approval. Identifying the competent substantial evidence on the record supports this argument.

The doctors and nurses at Safe Hospital hooked her up to a fetal-heart monitor and made the determination that the baby was still doing fine, and would continue to monitor. Over the next two hours as Sara was in active labor, the fetal monitoring records demonstrated decelerations, bradycardia, and tachycardia.

Eventually, when the heart rate had dropped to a dangerously low level, the doctor began attempts to manually deliver through the use of forceps and vacuum. Ultimately he was successful in getting Baby Davis out, however, at birth, Baby Davis demonstrated low APGAR scores, need for resuscitation, and neurological intervention. 

The family was shook by the delivery process and even though Baby Davis was not in good condition, they had him transferred to the Lurie’s Children’s Hospital in Cook County, Illinois. Baby Davis underwent extensive surgical and medical intervention for the next 23 days until he almost passed away on September 16, 2024.
